title: A Look at Metamorphosis Alpha
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SKEcZIJKPzc

A viewer named Adam donated the Goodman Games deluxe edition of Metamorphosis Alpha, and Daniel (@dungeondive) uses it to trace a personal lineage. Growing up during the first satanic panic he was forbidden Dungeons & Dragons, so Gamma World, bought at Arthur's Toys in Fresno, became his first RPG love; he still rolls the d10s from that box, corners worn round after more than thirty years. Metamorphosis Alpha is where Gamma World came from: James M. Ward's 1976 game, written under Gary Gygax at TSR and generally credited as the first science-fiction RPG, set aboard the lost starship Warden whose mutant and human natives do not know they are on a ship, an idea lifted from Brian Aldiss's Non-Stop.

The deluxe volume reproduces the original as scans with page numbers intact, so the reprinted Dragon articles still point to the right pages, and cross-references every piece of errata. He reads from Ward's interview, a 1977 review whose only complaint is the "god awful cover" he adores, a bionics supplement with a bizarrely grumpy opening, an alternate clone-based start he would use, and a newcomer's account of mailing five dollars for a flimsy booklet. He is candid that he will never actually play it: truly old-school games were complex, not simple, and Ward's insistence that players not metagame runs against how Daniel likes to play. He treasures the book anyway, and eyes the new introductory adventure for a solo run.

----

Daniel argues that genuinely old-school games were far more complex than the modern OSR imagines. Do you agree, and which vintage rulebook proved it to you?
